newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Alitalia joins line of EU airline state-aid probes.
newsitem.headline: Alitalia joins line of EU airline state-aid probes.

text.p: The European Commission launched its latest airline state-aid probe on Wednesday after rejecting Italian carrier Alitalia's case for a three trillion lire bail-out partly funded by the Rome government.

"The Commission today decided to open a procedure under article 93(2) of the Treaty to investigate whether the proposed capital injection of 1500 billion lire by the Institution for Industrial Reconstruction in the airline Alitalia is compatible with the Treaty rules regarding state aid in the aviation sector," it said in statement IP/96/908.

Alitalia told the Commission of its intended cash injection last July, saying that 1.5 trillion lire ($990 million) would be paid by its largest shareholder, the state-owned holding company Istituto per la Ricostruzione Industriale (IRI).
Italian authorities said that in making such a payment, IRI was acting as any private investor would and therefore the money did not come under the EU's state aid rules.
"At this stage, the Commission is not convinced by these arguments in view of the present situation of the company and of the restructuring plan submitted by Italy," it said.
The Commission rejected this on the grounds that Alitalia's private investors, who hold 10 percent of the airline stock, showed no indication of stumping up any money.
It added that the second instalment of 1.5 trillion lire, due in 1997, was "not covered by the sort of guarantees a private investor might be expected to demand".

A Commission official told Reuters that there had been some confusion as to the source of this second payment. Initial indications from Rome that it would be sourced privately now appeared to have been contradicted by Italy's recent budget, which suggested IRI would pay. This would be another element of the probe, the official said.

The Commission gave details of Alitalia's planned restructuring package, a two-phased effort running from 1996 to 1997 and from 1998 to 2000. The first step would be to clear up the company's financial operations and the second to secure its medium to long-term development.
Alitalia plans to supplement two payments of 1.5 trillion lire in 1996 and 1997 with an offer for employees to buy 313 billion lire of stock over the same period.
"This is accompanied by cuts in ground staff, a new salary structure and further cost-cutting reductions such as the sale of non-strategic subsidiaries such as Alfa Romeo Avio," it said.

Wednesday's move brings Alitalia into a long line of companies that have been targets of Commission state aid investigations including state-owned carriers such as Spain's Iberia, Air France, Greece's Olympic Airways, Ireland's Aer Lingus, and TAP Air Portugal.
In the end, the Commission approved all the previous cases but with conditions such as enforced sell-offs of certain holdings and limits on fare-cutting and new capacity.
A senior Commission official told Reuters that the Italian authorities' current argument that the money was not state aid might indicate why the airline had not been looked at earlier.
"They may have received aid before, but there's no way the Commission could have known unless it had been alerted by a competitor or by other means," the official said.
"There's no reason to assume this will be a quick process," the official added.
Last week, rival airline British Airways said it would complain to the Commission over what it called unfair aid to Alitalia.
